questions.question: What is the fundamental objective of Regression Testing?

options.A: To retest software after modifications to confirm that new bugs or regressions have not been introduced into existing, previously working features.
options.C: To test the software only once before deletion.
options.D: To revert the software to version 1.0.

questions.explanation: Regression testing ensures that code modifications (bug fixes, enhancements, refactoring) do not unintentionally break existing functionality.

questions.question: What is the 'Retest-All' regression testing strategy?

options.A: Re-running every single test case in the entire test suite on every modified build.
options.B: Writing all tests again from scratch.

questions.explanation: The Retest-All strategy re-executes the entire existing test suite indiscriminately. While safe, it becomes prohibitively slow and expensive as suites grow.

questions.question: What is Regression Test Selection (RTS)?

options.A: Selecting a relevant subset of existing test cases that execute the modified parts of the software or components affected by the changes.
options.C: Selecting tests based on author names.
options.D: Deleting test cases that take more than 1 second.

questions.explanation: RTS algorithms analyze source code diffs or impact graphs to identify and execute only those test cases whose execution traces traverse modified code.

questions.question: What is a 'Safe' Regression Test Selection technique?

options.A: An RTS technique that guarantees selecting every test case in the suite that could possibly reveal a fault in the modified program (under certain standard assumptions).
options.B: A technique that never runs tests.
options.C: A technique that encrypts test scripts.
options.D: A technique that runs in an isolated sandbox.

questions.explanation: A safe RTS algorithm guarantees that any test case capable of producing a different output between the original and modified version will be included in the selected test subset.

questions.question: What is Test Suite Minimization (TSM) / Test Suite Reduction?

options.A: Permanently identifying and removing redundant test cases from the test suite while preserving coverage of all test requirements.

questions.explanation: Test Suite Minimization removes redundant tests that cover requirements already satisfied by other tests, permanently reducing maintenance overhead.

questions.question: What is Test Case Prioritization (TCP)?

options.A: Re-ordering test cases so that those with higher likelihood of revealing faults or higher code coverage are executed earlier in the test run.

questions.explanation: Test Case Prioritization schedules tests in an optimal execution order to maximize the rate of fault detection, giving developers rapid feedback on breakages.

questions.question: What metric is standardly used to evaluate the effectiveness of Test Case Prioritization schedules?

options.A: APFD (Average Percentage of Faults Detected)

questions.explanation: APFD measures how quickly a prioritized test suite reveals faults: higher APFD values indicate that faults are detected earlier in the test execution cycle.

questions.question: What is the formula for APFD (Average Percentage of Faults Detected) for n tests and m faults, where TFi is the index of the first test that detects fault i?
questions.explanation: The standard APFD formula is: APFD = 1 - (TF1 + TF2 + ... + TFm) / (n × m) + 1 / (2n). It ranges from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%).

questions.question: Suppose a test suite of 5 tests {T1, T2, T3, T4, T5} detects 2 faults. If the faults are detected by T1 (position 1) and T2 (position 2), what is the APFD?
What is a 'flaky test' in regression testing?

options.A: A test that exhibits both passing and failing outcomes across different runs on the exact same version of code without any source changes.
options.B: A test that takes less than 1 ms.
options.D: A test that tests floating-point numbers.

questions.explanation: Flaky tests exhibit non-deterministic results due to race conditions, timing issues, network latencies, or order dependencies, undermining developer trust in CI.

questions.question: In Regression Test Selection, what is the 'analysis cost vs execution cost' tradeoff?

options.A: If the time required to perform dependency/impact analysis to select tests exceeds the execution time saved by skipping tests, RTS provides no net benefit.
options.C: Analysis cost only applies to cloud testing.
options.D: Execution cost is always higher than analysis cost.

questions.explanation: For RTS to be economically viable: Cost(Analysis) + Cost(Selected Tests) must be strictly less than Cost(Retest-All). For very small suites, Retest-All is faster.

questions.question: What is 'Code Churn' in regression testing analysis?

options.A: The volume of lines of code added, modified, or deleted between two software versions.
options.B: The rotation speed of a hard disk.
options.C: The frequency of developer coffee breaks.
options.D: The number of comments in a file.

questions.explanation: High code churn (frequent edits across many files) indicates high change instability and correlates strongly with regression defect density.

questions.question: What is 'Change Impact Analysis'?

options.A: Techniques that determine the potential ripple effects and affected dependencies resulting from a proposed modification to software.
options.C: Measuring the download speed of git clone.
options.D: Checking disk space before writing code.

questions.explanation: Impact analysis traces data and call dependencies from changed code to identify all callers, data structures, and downstream features that could be influenced.

questions.question: How does Test Case Prioritization based on 'Total Statement Coverage' differ from 'Additional Statement Coverage'?

options.A: Total coverage orders tests by overall statements covered; Additional coverage iteratively picks the test that covers the maximum number of statements NOT YET covered by previously chosen tests.
options.B: Total coverage deletes tests; Additional coverage adds new tests.
options.C: They produce the identical ordering in all cases.
options.D: Additional coverage requires running tests in reverse.

questions.explanation: Total prioritization picks tests greedily by total coverage. Additional prioritization dynamically recalculates coverage, selecting tests that maximize marginal coverage gain.

questions.question: What is the primary risk of aggressive Test Suite Minimization (TSM)?

options.A: Minimization permanently removes tests that are redundant for a specific coverage metric (e.g. branch coverage), but those removed tests might have detected future regression faults.
options.B: Minimization makes the test suite run too fast.

questions.explanation: Two tests might cover the same branch with different inputs. Minimizing one test preserves branch coverage, but sacrifices fault-detection capability for other subtle bugs.

questions.question: What role does Continuous Integration (CI) play in modern regression testing?

options.A: It automatically builds and runs regression tests upon every code commit or pull request, giving immediate regression feedback to developers.
options.B: It replaces manual code reviews with automated deployment.
options.C: It eliminates the need for unit testing.
options.D: It prevents developers from committing code.

questions.explanation: CI platforms (e.g. GitHub Actions, Jenkins) automate test execution on every change, detecting regression bugs within minutes of commit.

questions.question: What is 'test order dependency' in regression test execution?

options.A: When test B only passes if test A runs before it (due to shared mutable state or database side-effects).
options.C: Running unit tests before integration tests.
options.D: Executing tests on a single CPU core.

questions.explanation: Order dependency occurs when tests are not cleanly isolated and leak state, causing tests to pass or fail depending on the sequence in which they execute.

questions.question: What is a 'regression test oracle'?

options.A: A mechanism (such as golden master outputs, assertions, or diff comparisons) that verifies current execution results against expected correct behavior.
options.C: A machine learning model predicting stock prices.

questions.explanation: An oracle determines whether test execution produced the expected behavior, flagging regressions when discrepancies emerge.

questions.question: Why is history-based test prioritization (prioritizing tests that failed recently or test frequently modified files) effective?

options.A: Empirical evidence shows that faults cluster in recently modified code and in components that have historically failed.
options.C: Because recent files have smaller sizes.
options.D: Because historical tests take less time to execute.

questions.explanation: Defect clustering and churn correlation mean tests touching recently modified or historically buggy components have a significantly higher likelihood of finding new regressions.

questions.question: What is 'smoke testing' in the context of regression test suites?

options.A: A quick preliminary subset of critical tests executed first to verify that core builds and basic functionalities work before running exhaustive regression suites.
options.C: Stress testing until the server overheats.

questions.explanation: Smoke tests (or build verification tests) verify fundamental sanity. If basic smoke tests fail, the build is rejected immediately without wasting time on full regression runs.
